claim: SNX4 is an evolutionary conserved organizer of membrane recycling.
source: Sorting nexin 4 (SNX4) is an evolutionary conserved organizer of membrane recycling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about SNX4.

claim: In neurons, SNX4 accumulates in synapses.
source: In neurons, SNX4 accumulates in synapses, but how SNX4 affects synapse function remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior literature cited in the introduction.

claim: SNX4 cKO synapses show enhanced neurotransmission during train stimulation.
source: We generated a conditional SNX4 knock-out mouse model and report that SNX4 cKO synapses show enhanced neurotransmission during train stimulation, while the first evoked EPSC was normal.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The first evoked EPSC was normal in SNX4 cKO synapses.
source: We generated a conditional SNX4 knock-out mouse model and report that SNX4 cKO synapses show enhanced neurotransmission during train stimulation, while the first evoked EPSC was normal.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 2b-d.

claim: SNX4 depletion did not affect vesicle recycling.
source: SNX4 depletion did not affect vesicle recycling, basic autophagic flux, or the levels and localization of SNARE-protein VAMP2/synaptobrevin-2.
evidence: This is supported by SypHy and FM4-64 dye experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: SNX4 depletion did not affect basic autophagic flux.
source: SNX4 depletion did not affect vesicle recycling, basic autophagic flux, or the levels and localization of SNARE-protein VAMP2/synaptobrevin-2.
evidence: This is supported by P62 and bafilomycin experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SNX4 depletion did not affect the levels and localization of SNARE-protein VAMP2/synaptobrevin-2.
source: SNX4 depletion did not affect vesicle recycling, basic autophagic flux, or the levels and localization of SNARE-protein VAMP2/synaptobrevin-2.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry and western blot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: SNX4 depletion caused an increase in docked synaptic vesicles at the active zone.
source: However, SNX4 depletion affected synapse ultrastructure: an increase in docked synaptic vesicles at the active zone, while the overall vesicle number was normal, and a decreased active zone length.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The overall vesicle number was normal in SNX4 cKO synapses.
source: However, SNX4 depletion affected synapse ultrastructure: an increase in docked synaptic vesicles at the active zone, while the overall vesicle number was normal, and a decreased active zone length.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: SNX4 depletion caused a decreased active zone length.
source: However, SNX4 depletion affected synapse ultrastructure: an increase in docked synaptic vesicles at the active zone, while the overall vesicle number was normal, and a decreased active zone length.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: SNX4 depletion leads to a substantially increased density of docked vesicles per release site.
source: These effects together lead to a substantially increased density of docked vesicles per release site.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: SNX4 is a negative regulator of synaptic vesicle docking and release.
source: In conclusion, SNX4 is a negative regulator of synaptic vesicle docking and release.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined electrophysiology and electron microscopy data.

claim: SNX4 has a role in synaptic vesicle recruitment at the active zone.
source: These findings suggest a role for SNX4 in synaptic vesicle recruitment at the active zone.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced neurotransmission during train stimulation and increased docked vesicles.

claim: Endosome sorting plays a critical role in the recycling and degradation of proteins in neurons.
source: Endosome sorting plays a critical role in the recycling and degradation of proteins in various eukaryotic cell types, including neurons (Cullen and Steinberg, 2018; Huotari and Helenius, 2011; Sardana and Emr, 2021; Vietri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Synapses rely on rapid recycling mechanisms to replenish synaptic vesicles and facilitate neurotransmitter release.
source: Synapses, in particular, rely on rapid recycling mechanisms to replenish synaptic vesicles (SVs) and facilitate neurotransmitter release (Kononenko and Haucke, 2015; Rizzoli, 2014; Südhof, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Depleting endosomal proteins affects neurotransmitter release.
source: While it has been demonstrated that depleting endosomal proteins affect neurotransmitter release (Chen et al., 2017; Tagliatti et al., 2016; Uytterhoeven et al., 2011), the precise role of these sorting proteins on SV maintenance and fusogenity remains not well understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: SNX4 belongs to a subgroup of SNXs containing a C-terminal Bin-Amphiphysin-Rvs (BAR) domain that recognizes and remodels curved endosome membranes.
source: SNX4 belongs to a subgroup of SNXs containing a C-terminal Bin-Amphiphysin-Rvs (BAR) domain that recognizes and remodels curved endosome membranes (Cullen and Steinberg, 2018; Teasdale et al., 2001; van Weering et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SNX4 forms a distinct sorting complex with SNX7, SNX30, SNX5, or SNX32 for endosome-to-cell surface recycling pathways and autophagosome traffic.
source: SNX4 forms a distinct sorting complex with SNX7, SNX30 (Antón et al., 2020; van Weering et al., 2012b), SNX5 (Zhou et al., 2022), or SNX32 (Sugatha et al., 2023) for endosome-to-cell surface recycling pathways and autophagosome traffic (Traer et al., 2007; van Weering et al., 2012a; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The expression of SNX4 is required for the stable SNX7 and SNX30 protein levels in cells.
source: SNX4 emerges as a central hub in this endosome recycling pathway as the expression of SNX4 is required for the stable SNX7 and SNX30 protein levels in cells (Antón et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Altered protein levels of SNX4 have been observed in post-mortem brain material of Alzheimer's disease patients.
source: In post-mortem brain material of Alzheimer's disease patients, altered protein levels of SNX4 have been observed (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SNX4 is implicated in the recycling of the amyloid precursor protein cleaving enzyme (BACE-1), sorting it away from the endolysosomal pathway.
source: SNX4 is implicated in the recycling of the amyloid precursor protein cleaving enzyme (BACE-1), sorting it away from the endolysosomal pathway (Kim et al., 2017; Toh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dysregulation of SNX4 may lead to the mislocalization of BACE-1 to late endosomal compartments, potentially contributing to altered amyloid-β-production.
source: Consequently, dysregulation of SNX4 may lead to the mislocalization of BACE-1 to late endosomal compartments, potentially contributing to altered amyloid-β-production.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of SNX4 in BACE-1 recycling.

claim: In yeast, Snx4 is essential for the endosome recycling of Snc1p, a homologue of the SNARE-protein VAMP2/synaptobrevin-2.
source: In yeast, Snx4 is essential for the endosome recycling of Snc1p, a homologue of the SNARE-protein VAMP2/synaptobrevin-2 (VAMP2/syb2) that is essential for synaptic transmission (Hettema et al., 2003; Ma et al., 2017; Schoch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SNX4 knockdown dysregulates protein pathways involved in neurotransmission in neurons.
source: In neurons, SNX4 specifically accumulates in synapses, and its knockdown dysregulates protein pathways involved in neurotransmission (Vazquez-Sanchez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SNX4 has a half lifetime of 10.6 days in neuronal cultures.
source: In neuronal cultures, SNX4 has a half lifetime of 10.6 days (Dörrbaum et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SNX4 expression was reduced by 67% after 14 days of Cre expression.
source: SNX4 expression was detected by western blot which showed a reduction of 67% after 14 days of Cre, 83% after 18 days of Cre, and 90% after 21 days of Cre compared to control neurons infected with delta-Cre (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: SNX4 expression was reduced by 83% after 18 days of Cre expression.
source: SNX4 expression was detected by western blot which showed a reduction of 67% after 14 days of Cre, 83% after 18 days of Cre, and 90% after 21 days of Cre compared to control neurons infected with delta-Cre (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: SNX4 expression was reduced by 90% after 21 days of Cre expression.
source: SNX4 expression was detected by western blot which showed a reduction of 67% after 14 days of Cre, 83% after 18 days of Cre, and 90% after 21 days of Cre compared to control neurons infected with delta-Cre (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: Immunohistochemistry showed a 64% reduction in SNX4 in MAP2-neurites after 21 days of expressing Cre.
source: Immunohistochemistry of SNX4 in primary hippocampal neurons showed a 64% reduction in SNX4 in MAP2-neurites after 21 days of expressing Cre (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1e and f.

claim: Dendrite length remained unaffected in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: Morphological parameters such as dendrite length and dendrite branching, based on MAP2 staining, and synapse number, based on VAMP2 puncta, remained unaffected in SNX4 cKO neurons (Figure 1f–i and Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Dendrite branching remained unaffected in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: Morphological parameters such as dendrite length and dendrite branching, based on MAP2 staining, and synapse number, based on VAMP2 puncta, remained unaffected in SNX4 cKO neurons (Figure 1f–i and Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Synapse number remained unaffected in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: Morphological parameters such as dendrite length and dendrite branching, based on MAP2 staining, and synapse number, based on VAMP2 puncta, remained unaffected in SNX4 cKO neurons (Figure 1f–i and Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by synapse counting shown in Figure 1i.

claim: The amplitude of the first evoked response showed a non-significant trend toward an increase in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: Both the amplitude and charge of the first evoked response showed a non-significant trend toward an increase in SNX4 cKO neurons (KO) compared to neurons infected with delta-Cre (control) (Figure 2b, c, and d).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The charge of the first evoked response showed a non-significant trend toward an increase in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: Both the amplitude and charge of the first evoked response showed a non-significant trend toward an increase in SNX4 cKO neurons (KO) compared to neurons infected with delta-Cre (control) (Figure 2b, c, and d).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The rescue condition where SNX4 was re-expressed at DIV14 showed a decreased amplitude compared to KO but not to control.
source: The rescue condition where SNX4 was re-expressed at DIV14 (KO+SNX4) showed a decreased amplitude compared to KO but not to control.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Paired pulse ratios were not affected in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: Paired pulse ratios were not affected in SNX4 cKO neurons (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: During a train of 100 action potentials at 40 Hz, the charge in SNX4 cKO neurons was highly increased.
source: During a train of 100 action potentials (APs) at 40 Hz, the charge in SNX4 cKO neurons was highly increased (Figure 2f and h).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2f and h.

claim: The average charge between pulse 90 and 100 was increased by 110% in SNX4 cKO synapses compared to control.
source: The average charge between pulse 90 and 100 was increased by 110% in SNX4 cKO synapses compared to control (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: SNX4 overexpression rescued the increase in charge to wild-type levels.
source: SNX4 overexpression rescued this increase in charge to wild-type (WT) levels (Figure 2f, g, and h).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2f, g, and h.

claim: No significant differences in RRP estimate size were found in SNX4 cKO synapses compared to control.
source: While we found no significant differences in RRP estimate size in SNX4 cKO synapses compared to control (Figure 2i), the slope estimate of the cumulative charge was increased upon SNX4 depletion, which was rescued by SNX4 overexpression (Figure 2j).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: The slope estimate of the cumulative charge was increased upon SNX4 depletion.
source: While we found no significant differences in RRP estimate size in SNX4 cKO synapses compared to control (Figure 2i), the slope estimate of the cumulative charge was increased upon SNX4 depletion, which was rescued by SNX4 overexpression (Figure 2j).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: The amplitude of spontaneous miniature EPSCs was not affected upon SNX4 depletion.
source: The amplitude and frequency of spontaneous miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs) were not affected upon SNX4 depletion (Figure 2k–m).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2l.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous miniature EPSCs was not affected upon SNX4 depletion.
source: The amplitude and frequency of spontaneous miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs) were not affected upon SNX4 depletion (Figure 2k–m).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2m.

claim: SNX4 overexpression in itself does not affect the neurotransmission protocols studied in SNX4 cKO experiments.
source: Both the amplitude and charge of the first evoked response showed no effect in control+SNX4 neurons compared to control, and no differences were detected in the response to the 40 Hz stimulation train (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–e), indicating that SNX4 overexpression in itself does not affect the neurotransmission protocols studied in SNX4 cKO experiments.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–e.

claim: Vesicle recruitment during high-frequency train stimulation is limited by SNX4.
source: Together these data show enhanced neurotransmission during train stimulation in SNX4 cKO autapses, while single EPSCs, mEPSCs, and the RRP size estimate remain unaffected. This suggests that vesicle recruitment during high-frequency train stimulation is limited by SNX4.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined electrophysiology data.

claim: Different SV recycling pathways dominate at different temperatures.
source: It has, however, been shown that different SV recycling pathways dominate at different temperatures (Watanabe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SNX4 cKO neurons showed a higher fluorescence intensity upon both stimulation trains in SypHy experiments.
source: SNX4 cKO neurons showed a higher fluorescence intensity upon both stimulation trains (Figure 3c), represented as the stimulated fraction (Figure 3d and e), and return to baseline fluorescence level within 60 s over a total imaging time course of 160 s (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by SypHy imaging data shown in Figure 3c-e.

claim: The fluorescence decay time constant tau was not changed after both stimuli in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: The fluorescence decay time constant tau in the 60 s after electrical stimulation, a measure for SV endocytosis, was not changed after both stimuli in SNX4 cKO neurons (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by SypHy imaging data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The percentage of active synapses showed a trend toward fewer active synapses in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: Finally, the responding fluorescent puncta during AP stimulation as a ratio of the total fluorescent puncta during NH4, the percentage of active synapses, showed a trend toward fewer active synapses in SNX4 cKO neurons (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is supported by SypHy imaging data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: SNX4 depletion enhances SV release without altering SV recycling and the number of active synapses in hippocampal neurons.
source: Hence, these data show that SNX4 depletion enhances SV release without altering SV recycling and the number of active synapses in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the SypHy imaging data.

claim: SNX4 cKO neurons showed a similar fluorescence intensity decay after electrical stimulation in FM4-64 experiments.
source: SNX4 cKO neurons showed a similar fluorescence intensity decay after electrical stimulation over a total imaging time course of 80 s (Figure 3j).
evidence: This is supported by FM4-64 imaging data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: The average fluorescence signal in the last 10 s normalized to baseline was not significantly different between control and SNX4 cKO neurons in FM4-64 experiments.
source: The average fluorescence signal in the last 10 s normalized to baseline (F/F0), a measure for the total amount of recycling SVs fusing, was not significantly different between control and SNX4 cKO neurons (Figure 3k).
evidence: This is supported by FM4-64 imaging data shown in Figure 3k.

claim: FM4-64 uptake was not altered in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: FM4-64 uptake, a measure for endocytosis at 37°C, was also not altered in SNX4 cKO neurons (Figure 3l).
evidence: This is supported by FM4-64 imaging data shown in Figure 3l.

claim: SNX4 depletion does not affect SV endocytosis and recycling at both room temperature and physiological temperature.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that SNX4 depletion does not affect SV endocytosis and recycling at both room temperature and physiological temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined SypHy and FM4-64 imaging data.

claim: SNX4 immunostaining showed clear co-localization with VAMP2/syb-2.
source: SNX4 immunostaining showed clear co-localization with VAMP2/syb-2 (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: No significant difference was found in VAMP2/syb-2 puncta number per µm dendrite in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: In SNX4 cKO neurons, no significant difference was found in VAMP2/syb-2 puncta number per µm dendrite or VAMP2/syb-2 intensity (Figure 4a, b, and c).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: No significant difference was found in VAMP2/syb-2 intensity in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: In SNX4 cKO neurons, no significant difference was found in VAMP2/syb-2 puncta number per µm dendrite or VAMP2/syb-2 intensity (Figure 4a, b, and c).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Sholl analysis revealed no differences in VAMP2/syb-2 localization upon SNX4 depletion.
source: Sholl analysis of average VAMP2/syb-2 intensity over distance from soma also revealed no differences in VAMP2/syb-2 localization upon SNX4 depletion (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed no changes in total VAMP2/syb-2 protein levels.
source: Western blot analysis revealed no changes in total VAMP2/syb-2 protein levels (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: SNX4 is not required for a normal VAMP2/syb-2 distribution and protein level.
source: These data show that SNX4 is not required for a normal VAMP2/syb-2 distribution and protein level, as observed for the yeast orthologs of both proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the VAMP2 immunocytochemistry and western blot data.

claim: There was no significant difference in P62 puncta numbers in SNX4 cKO neurons under basal conditions or after bafilomycin treatment.
source: In SNX4 cKO neurons, there was no significant difference in P62 puncta numbers or P62 somatic intensity under basal conditions or after bafilomycin treatment, suggesting that autophagic flux remains normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by P62 immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: There was no significant difference in P62 somatic intensity in SNX4 cKO neurons under basal conditions or after bafilomycin treatment.
source: In SNX4 cKO neurons, there was no significant difference in P62 puncta numbers or P62 somatic intensity under basal conditions or after bafilomycin treatment, suggesting that autophagic flux remains normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by P62 immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Autophagic flux remains normal in SNX4 cKO neurons.
source: In SNX4 cKO neurons, there was no significant difference in P62 puncta numbers or P62 somatic intensity under basal conditions or after bafilomycin treatment, suggesting that autophagic flux remains normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is inferred from the P62 and bafilomycin data.

claim: Western blot analysis showed no changes in total ATG5 protein levels.
source: Western blot analysis also showed no changes in total ATG5 protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e) and ultrastructural analysis revealed no differences in the total number of autophagosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f and g).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: Ultrastructural analysis revealed no differences in the total number of autophagosomes.
source: Western blot analysis also showed no changes in total ATG5 protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e) and ultrastructural analysis revealed no differences in the total number of autophagosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f and g).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f and g.

claim: SNX4 depletion does not impact the basal autophagic flux, ATG5 protein levels, or the number of autophagosomes.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that SNX4 depletion does not impact the basal autophagic flux, ATG5 protein levels, or the number of autophagosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined autophagy marker data.

claim: The average SV size was reduced by 5% in SNX4 cKO synapses.
source: The average SV size, defined by all clear core vesicles smaller than 50 nm, was reduced by 5%, whereas vesicles larger than 50 nm did not show significant changes upon SNX4 depletion (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Vesicles larger than 50 nm did not show significant changes upon SNX4 depletion.
source: The average SV size, defined by all clear core vesicles smaller than 50 nm, was reduced by 5%, whereas vesicles larger than 50 nm did not show significant changes upon SNX4 depletion (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The distribution of vesicles, grouped by bin size of 10 nm, showed no notable differences upon SNX4 depletion.
source: Additionally, the distribution of vesicles, grouped by bin size of 10 nm, showed no notable differences upon SNX4 depletion. (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of docked vesicles was significantly higher in SNX4 cKO synapses than in control.
source: In SNX4 cKO synapses, the number of docked vesicles was significantly higher than in control (Figure 5a and f) while the total number of vesicles was not altered (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The density of docked vesicles at the active zone length increases by 50% in SNX4 cKO synapses compared to control.
source: When normalized to the active zone length, the density of docked vesicles at the active zone length further increases by 50% in SNX4 cKO synapses compared to control (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: A significant decrease in active zone length was observed in SNX4 cKO synapses.
source: Moreover, we observed a significant decrease in active zone length, PSD length, and vesicle cluster area (Figure 5g–j).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: A significant decrease in PSD length was observed in SNX4 cKO synapses.
source: Moreover, we observed a significant decrease in active zone length, PSD length, and vesicle cluster area (Figure 5g–j).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5i.

claim: A significant decrease in vesicle cluster area was observed in SNX4 cKO synapses.
source: Moreover, we observed a significant decrease in active zone length, PSD length, and vesicle cluster area (Figure 5g–j).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5j.

claim: SNX4 depletion affects the presynaptic ultrastructure, characterized by smaller active zone length and vesicle cluster area, suggesting a decrease in overall synapse size.
source: Together these data show that SNX4 depletion affects the presynaptic ultrastructure, characterized by smaller active zone length and vesicle cluster area, suggesting a decrease in overall synapse size.
evidence: This is inferred from the electron microscopy data.

claim: In smaller synapses, SNX4 cKO neurons contain more docked SVs leading to a substantially increased density of docked vesicles per release site.
source: In these smaller synapses, SNX4 cKO neurons contain more docked SVs leading to a substantially increased density of docked vesicles per release site.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined electron microscopy data on docked vesicles and active zone length.

claim: Increased neurotransmission upon depletion of endosomal genes has been shown by several labs.
source: Increased neurotransmission upon depletion of endosomal genes has been shown by several labs (Fernandes et al., 2014; Soykan et al., 2021; Tagliatti et al., 2016; Uytterhoeven et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Endosomes act as sorting stations for SV proteins and control the balance between novel and reused SV proteins that affect SV release and neurotransmission efficiency.
source: These results are consistent with a postulated hypothesis that endosomes act as sorting stations for SV proteins and control the balance between novel and reused SV proteins that affect SV release and neurotransmission efficiency (Fernandes et al., 2014; Truckenbrodt et al., 2018; Uytterhoeven et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the presence of SNX4, the recycling process may lead to the reuse of older SV proteins that potentially diminish the efficiency of SV exocytosis.
source: In the presence of SNX4, the recycling process may lead to the reuse of older SV proteins that, as indirect consequence, potentially diminish the efficiency of SV exocytosis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: In the absence of SNX4, older SV proteins are less recycled and traffic toward degradation, rendering the synapse with relatively more novel SV proteins, enhancing SV recruitment and fusion.
source: In the absence of SNX4, older SV proteins are less recycled and traffic toward degradation, rendering the synapse with relatively more novel SV proteins, enhancing SV recruitment and fusion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Blocking the degradation pathway with HOPS/ESCRT mutants rescues the observed increased release.
source: Blocking the degradation pathway with HOPS/ESCRT mutants rescues the observed increased release (Fernandes et al., 2014; Uytterhoeven et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Skywalker and ARF6 mutants show increased SV sorting through endosomal intermediates, increasing SV docking and release.
source: Similarly, Skywalker and ARF6 mutants show increased SV sorting through endosomal intermediates, increasing SV docking and release (Fernandes et al., 2014; Tagliatti et al., 2016; Uytterhoeven et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SNX4 cKO synapses do not show an accumulation of endosomal intermediates.
source: That said, SNX4 cKO synapses do not show an accumulation of endosomal intermediates (Figure 5d) or decreased SV numbers (Figure 5e) as reported for other endosome gene mutants, marking a novel finding in endosomal protein knock-out studies.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: SNX4 cKO synapses do not show decreased SV numbers as reported for other endosome gene mutants.
source: That said, SNX4 cKO synapses do not show an accumulation of endosomal intermediates (Figure 5d) or decreased SV numbers (Figure 5e) as reported for other endosome gene mutants, marking a novel finding in endosomal protein knock-out studies.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Endosomal sorting mediates the delivery of active zone proteins.
source: Endosomal sorting also mediates the delivery of active zone proteins, where disturbances in these pathways potentially correlate with smaller active zones and SVs, ultrastructural phenotypes were also observed in SNX4 cKO synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed ultrastructural changes in SNX4 cKO synapses.

claim: Disturbances in endosomal sorting pathways potentially correlate with smaller active zones and SVs.
source: Endosomal sorting also mediates the delivery of active zone proteins, where disturbances in these pathways potentially correlate with smaller active zones and SVs, ultrastructural phenotypes were also observed in SNX4 cKO synapses.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting endosomal sorting to the observed phenotypes.

claim: The removal of SNX4 directs its cargo toward the degradative pathway.
source: Previous studies suggest that the removal of SNX4 directs its cargo toward the degradative pathway (Hettema et al., 2003; Traer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SNX4 has been reported to regulate several types of autophagy.
source: Apart from endosome sorting, SNX4 has been reported to regulate several types of autophagy (Antón et al., 2020; Hanley et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SV release could be regulated by synaptic autophagy.
source: Recent literature has shown that SV release could be regulated by synaptic autophagy (reviewed by Decet and Verstreken, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Loss of ATG5 results in increased neurotransmission, an effect independent from total SVs pool number.
source: Loss of ATG5 has been shown to result in increased neurotransmission, an effect independent from total SVs pool number (Kuijpers et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: No changes in total ATG5 levels were observed upon SNX4 depletion, consistent with previous reports.
source: We did not observe changes in total ATG5 levels upon SNX4 depletion, consistent with previous reports (Antón et al., 2020), and no difference in basic autophagic flux of P62, contrasting with previous findings in HeLa cells (Antón et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and a citation to prior literature.

claim: No difference in basic autophagic flux of P62 was observed upon SNX4 depletion, contrasting with previous findings in HeLa cells.
source: We did not observe changes in total ATG5 levels upon SNX4 depletion, consistent with previous reports (Antón et al., 2020), and no difference in basic autophagic flux of P62, contrasting with previous findings in HeLa cells (Antón et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by P62 data and contrasted with a citation to prior literature.

claim: SNX4 may have a specialized role in neurons that regulates synaptic transmission independent of autophagic flux by a yet-to-be determined mechanism.
source: This suggests that SNX4 may have a specialized role in neurons, that regulates synaptic transmission independent of autophagic flux by a yet-to-be determined mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of autophagy phenotypes despite neurotransmission changes.

claim: The presence of redundant pathways compensating for SNX4 depletion is suggested, potentially involving other SNX-BAR complexes or endosomal sorting complexes.
source: This suggests the presence of redundant pathways compensating for SNX4 depletion, potentially involving other SNX-BAR complexes or endosomal sorting complexes like ESCPE, retriever, or retromer (Simonetti et al., 2023).
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of certain expected phenotypes.

claim: SNX7 and SNX30 are of potential interest for future research due to their ability to form selective complexes with SNX4.
source: Particularly SNX-BAR proteins, such as SNX7 and SNX30, are of potential interest for future research due to their ability to form selective complexes with SNX4 (Antón et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by a citation.

claim: The role of endosome sorting in the SV cycle is increasingly recognized through knock-out studies targeting various endosomal complexes.
source: The role of endosome sorting in the SV cycle is increasingly recognized through knock-out studies targeting various endosomal complexes, revealing changes in SV exocytosis, SV endocytosis, or endosome-like vesicle numbers (Chen et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2008; Inoshita et al., 2017; Tagliatti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: This is the first time that a protein from the highly evolutionary conserved SNX-BAR protein family, such as SNX4, is shown to regulate SV docking at the active zone and sustained SV release.
source: Our data supports this, showing for the first time that a protein from the highly evolutionary conserved SNX-BAR protein family, such as SNX4, regulates SV docking at the active zone and sustained SV release.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Endosomal sorting protein SNX4 regulates SVs recruitment at the active zone.
source: Taken together, we show that endosomal sorting protein SNX4 regulates SVs recruitment at the active zone.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on all the data presented.

claim: The precise regulation of vesicle availability is crucial for a synapse to effectively coordinate neurotransmission, a process heavily relying on endosome sorting mechanisms.
source: The precise regulation of vesicle availability is crucial for a synapse to effectively coordinate neurotransmission, a process heavily relying on endosome sorting mechanisms.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of the findings.

claim: An increase in docked SVs at the active zone implies, on average, a closer proximity to calcium channels and therefore a higher release probability.
source: However, an increase in docked SVs at the active zone also implies, on average, a closer proximity to calcium channels and therefore a higher release probability.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural changes observed.

claim: Measures of release probability were unaffected by SNX4 deficiency, suggesting a normal channel coupling in SNX4 cKO synapses.
source: However, measures of release probability were unaffected by SNX4 deficiency (as argued above), suggesting a normal channel coupling in SNX4 cKO synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the paired pulse ratio and other electrophysiology data.

claim: An increased contribution of newly recruited vesicles during sustained stimulation is consistent with the fact that neurotransmission is increased especially during high-frequency stimulation in SNX4 cKO synapses.
source: In line with this, the increased neurotransmission of SNX4 cKO neurons was less prominent in 5 and 10 Hz trains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Hence, an increased contribution of newly recruited vesicles during sustained stimulation is consistent with the fact that neurotransmission is increased especially during high-frequency stimulation in SNX4 cKO synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the frequency-dependent effects on neurotransmission.

claim: The increased neurotransmission of SNX4 cKO neurons was less prominent in 5 and 10 Hz trains.
source: In line with this, the increased neurotransmission of SNX4 cKO neurons was less prominent in 5 and 10 Hz trains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FM-64 dye method reports the release of only recycled vesicles.
source: The latter method reports the release of only recycled vesicles, suggesting that these do not contribute significantly to the enhanced release.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of the FM-64 dye method.

claim: Recycled vesicles do not contribute significantly to the enhanced release in SNX4 cKO synapses.
source: The latter method reports the release of only recycled vesicles, suggesting that these do not contribute significantly to the enhanced release.
evidence: This is inferred from the FM-64 dye data.

claim: The increased SV recruitment in SNX4 cKO synapses is not driven by an enhanced rate of the SV cycle.
source: Finally, examining SV recycling with FM-64 dye indicates that the increased SV recruitment in SNX4 cKO synapses is not driven by an enhanced rate of the SV cycle, as endocytosis and release of recycled SVs were normal in SNX4 cKO synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the FM-64 dye data.

claim: If more vesicles are already docked at the start of stimulation, they may on average be recruited faster during train stimulation.
source: If more vesicles are already docked at the start of stimulation, they may on average be recruited faster during train stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the docking data.

claim: SV docking is probably a dynamic equilibrium between various SV pools, modulated by activity.
source: SV docking is probably a dynamic equilibrium between various SV pools, modulated by activity (Kusick et al., 2020).
